title: Brandon Miller Is a Rorschach Test for NBA Talent Evaluation
contentHtml:
With the stunning trade of LaMelo Ball to the Minnesota Timberwolves finalized but not yet public on June 25, Jeff Peterson, the Charlotte Hornets president of basketball operations, called his two remaining franchise pillars—Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller—into the team’s Spectrum Center offices to tell them about the deal, Peterson recalled to The Lowe Post.

He wanted them to know before the news got out—to have a chance to digest the trade and perhaps their own increased prominence within the franchise. Both seemed slightly surprised, Peterson said. Miller told The Lowe Post that he had been with Ball earlier that day.

Hours later, the news shocked the NBA world. The Hornets had been the feel-good story of 2025-26, going 33-15 after January 2 and sporting the league’s best point differential in that stretch before falling to the Orlando Magic in the play-in tournament—admittedly an every-other-year fate for the franchise during the Ball era.

By the time the deal broke, Miller had already internalized it. “It was no surprise to me,” he told The Lowe Post. “But it was probably a surprise to you all. We knew what was going on. [Ball] is gonna continue to perfect his craft in Minnesota. As far as, is it a great fit for him? Is it a great move for us? I guess we’ll see. But I know his talent, and what he brings every night, and I think he’ll do great in Minnesota.”

By the numbers at least, Ball drove a lot of Charlotte’s winning last season. The Hornets outscored opponents by 9.1 points per 100 possessions with Ball on the floor, but that margin cratered to plus-1.5 when he sat, per NBA.com. Their offense fell apart when he hit the bench—even when both Knueppel and Miller remained on the floor, according to lineup data. By flipping Ball (and Josh Green) for Naz Reid and a bevy of picks and swaps, the Hornets appeared to be taking a step back for 2026-27 in order to better position the franchise to strike when Miller and Knueppel hit their primes.

The trade was a wager on Miller and Knueppel as potential stars; a bet that Coby White, acquired from the Chicago Bulls ahead of last season’s trade deadline, would provide some requisite percentage of Ball’s production at a lower salary and with more durability. It was also a hedge against Ball’s on-again, off-again injury issues, and perhaps an indication that Charlotte’s brain trust saw some fool’s gold in the team’s 50-game rampage over a league in which a third of the teams were tanking.

About three months after that trade, the Hornets reaffirmed their commitment to Miller by signing him to a five-year, $209 million extension—a hefty figure considering Miller had played only 166 games over three seasons before signing the deal. Given Charlotte’s trove of assets and the massive pivot point the Ball trade represents, it is not a stretch to say that Miller is one of the half dozen most important young players in the league—and maybe the most intriguing.

The Hornets’ surge last season coincided almost exactly with Miller’s return from an early-season shoulder injury, which dogged him all season and required surgery in the offseason. Miller played in 65 games after logging only 27 in his second season, which ended early due to wrist surgery. But as he rehabbed during that 2024-25 campaign, the Hornets made sure that Miller, the no. 2 pick in the 2023 draft ahead of the more ballyhooed Scoot Henderson, understood his importance to the franchise.

They had Miller shadow members of the coaching staff to understand their daily routines and how they watched film to scout opponents, according to Josh Longstaff, the Hornets assistant who works most closely with Miller. Miller did the same with the front office, even sitting in on meetings. And toward the end of that season, with Miller still out, he was called into a meeting with Peterson; Longstaff; Charles Lee, the team’s head coach; and a fourth person who was at one point the most important individual in the Hornets organization and the entire basketball world.
